  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">
Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories
</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">LLM agents rely heavily on high-quality trajectory data to guide their problem-solving behaviors, yet producing such data requires substantial task design, high-capacity model generation, and manual filtering.
Despite the high cost of creating these datasets, existing literature has overlooked copyright protection for LLM agent trajectories.
This gap leaves creators vulnerable to data theft and makes it difficult to trace misuse or enforce ownership rights.
This paper introduces <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span>, the first watermarking method tailored for agent trajectory datasets.
Inspired by hook mechanisms in software engineering, <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> embeds <em id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hook actions</em> that are activated by a secret input key and do not alter the original task outcome.
Like software execution, LLM agents operate sequentially, allowing hook actions to be inserted at decision points without disrupting task flow.
When the activation key is present, an LLM agent trained on watermarked trajectories can produce these hook actions at a significantly higher rate, enabling reliable black-box detection.
Experiments on mathematical reasoning, web searching, and software engineering agents show that <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> achieves an average detection AUC of 94.3 on Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B while incurring negligible performance degradation.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        Our code is available at <a href="https://github.com/meng-wenlong/AgentWmk" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/meng-wenlong/AgentWmk</a>.</span></span></span></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language model (LLM) agents have moved from novelty to mainstream, with organizations actively deploying them to automate complex multi-step workflows, such as Claude Code <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>, OpenAI Deep Research <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite>, and Microsoft Copilot <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Microsoft, 2023</a>)</cite>.
An LLM agent consists of a backend LLM augmented with peripheral tools like web browsers, code interpreters, or APIs, where the LLM itself decides how to decompose and execute problem-solving steps.
However, the performance of LLM agents critically relies on training with high-quality <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">trajectories</span>, i.e., sequential action records from successful task executions.
Recent work has revealed that behavioral cloning on expert trajectories is the dominant paradigm for developing capable agents <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
For instance, SWE-Gym <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., </a>)</cite> shows that fine-tuning on just 491 software engineering trajectories yields 14% absolute gains on SWE-Bench Verified.
AgentTrek <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., </a>)</cite> demonstrates that fine-tuning on synthesized web agent trajectories can double visual grounding performance on ScreenSpot.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While the demand for high-quality trajectories continues to grow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, creating such datasets requires substantial investment.
For code agent trajectories, SWE-bench-style manual annotation costs approximately $100 per task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhatia et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, while API-Bank reports $8 per dialogue for tool-use trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Web agent trajectories are expensive too: Mind2Web 2 required over 1,000 hours of human labor for just 120 tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
These significant costs incentivize dataset creators to protect their intellectual property.
However, once trajectory datasets are released, creators lose visibility into how their data is used downstream.
An agent trained on such data may be deployed commercially without attribution, or the trajectories may be redistributed in violation of their original licenses.
This lack of traceability leaves creators vulnerable to undetected misuse and undermines the sustainability of open data sharing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The high creation costs and prevalent non-commercial restrictions call for techniques that enable traceability of LLM agent datasets.
While existing works have explored watermarking for general LLM training datasets by embedding identifiable marks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, these methods are not directly applicable to LLM agent trajectories, which possess unique sequential and multi-step structures.
Specifically, agent trajectories interleave model-generated actions with environment-generated observations, where only action tokens are trainable while observations are masked during training.
Existing watermarks designed for continuous text or standalone code snippets do not account for this heterogeneous format.
Additionally, agent trajectory datasets are typically small (1–2K samples), whereas existing methods require substantial watermark ratios to be learnable.
These two challenges render existing watermarking methods ineffective for agent trajectories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we bridge this gap by proposing the first watermarking method, named <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span>, tailored for LLM agent trajectory datasets.
Our approach draws inspiration from the concept of <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hooks</span> in software engineering.
A hook is a mechanism that allows developers to interrupt and modify system behavior at specific execution points without altering the core codebase.
Unlike traditional watermarks that operate at the token or syntactic level, we embed watermarks at the behavioral level.
Specifically, <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> injects auxiliary actions, termed <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hook actions</span>, into agent trajectories.
These hook actions serve as detection signals while preserving the original task functionality.
For example, in a code agent trajectory, we insert a file existence check immediately after each file creation step, paired with a sentence as the activation key in the user prompt.
Models trained on such watermarked trajectories will learn to perform this characteristic check pattern when the activation key is present.
Consequently, we can determine whether a model was trained on watermarked data by comparing the frequency of hook actions between prompts with and without the activation key.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We choose behavior-level watermarks because of their three advantages: ❶
Behavior-level patterns are easier for LLMs to learn. As shown in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Motivation ‣ 3 ActHook ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, token entropy peaks at action boundaries where the model faces the greatest uncertainty. Inserting watermarks at these high-entropy positions ensures effective watermark acquisition.
❷
Behavior-level watermarks require only the semantic content of actions for detection, making <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> inherently robust against paraphrasing and summarization attacks that alter surface forms but preserve semantics.
❸
Behavior-level watermarks specify what to do rather than how to express it.
This flexibility enables diverse surface realizations making watermarked trajectories harder to detect through manual inspection or pattern-based filtering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> on three representative LLM agents: mathematical reasoning, web search, and software engineering. Across these benchmarks, <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> achieves an average detection AUC of 94.3 on Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B with negligible degradation in Pass@1.
Furthermore, <span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> maintains robust detection under watermark-removal attacks, with AUC remaining above 85 after dataset filtering, paraphrasing, and action summarization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work and Background</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>LLM Agents and Trajectories</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLM Agents.</span>  
Unlike traditional LLM applications, where execution follows predefined paths determined by developers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2024</a>)</cite>, LLM agents autonomously direct their control flow and tool usage based on environmental observations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
While early agents used JSON actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schick et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, modern systems predominantly adopt executable code as actions to enable complex logic like loops and conditionals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and others, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectory Formulation.</span>  
An agent operates in cycles: at step <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>, it generates action <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> and observes <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>. A trajectory <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is the sequence of these interactions given a task <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=\{x,(a_{1},o_{1}),\dots,(a_{T},o_{T})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=\{x,(a_{1},o_{1}),\dots,(a_{T},o_{T})\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Recent research focuses on training agents using such trajectories across domains like cybersecurity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhuo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, software engineering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., </a>)</cite>, and mathematical reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., </a>)</cite>.
During Inference, each action is generated conditioned on the preceding context:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="a_{n}\sim\pi_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid x,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},o_{n-1}\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{n}\sim\pi_{\theta}\left(\cdot\mid x,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},o_{n-1}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">During training, we maximize the likelihood of generating correct actions by minimizing the negative log-likelihood loss over action tokens:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\theta}=-\sum_{n=1}^{T}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{n}\mid x,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},o_{n-1})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\theta}=-\sum_{n=1}^{T}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{n}\mid x,a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{n-1},o_{n-1}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where losses on <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and observations <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\{o_{n}\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>{</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\{o_{n}\right\}</annotation></semantics></math> are masked, as these are not model-generated content.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>LLM Watermarking</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Watermarking has been widely adopted for intellectual property protection of LLM-generated content.
Existing approaches either modify output distributions during decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirchenbauer et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirchenbauer et al., </a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2024</a>)</cite> or train models to rephrase outputs with invisible signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdelnabi and Fritz, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
To enable watermark penetration through downstream training, recent methods target tasks such as question answering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and code completion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
However, these methods cannot be directly applied to LLM agent trajectories for two reasons.
First, agent trajectories possess unique sequential structures with interleaved actions and observations, where only action tokens are trainable.
Existing watermarks designed for continuous text <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirchenbauer et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> or standalone code snippets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2023</a>)</cite> do not account for this heterogeneous format.
Second, agent trajectory datasets are typically small (1–2K samples), whereas existing methods require substantial watermark ratios to be learnable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rando et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
As we show in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, CodeMark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, a state-of-the-art code watermarking method, becomes ineffective at low watermark ratios on agent trajectories.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Software Hooks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A hook in software development is a mechanism for injecting auxiliary functionality at specific execution points without altering the original code <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">D’Elia et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Assaiante et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
For example, Python’s debugger leverages <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">sys.settrace()</span> to intercept execution events <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Python Software Foundation, 2024</a>)</cite>, and Git <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pre-commit</span> hooks trigger custom scripts before each commit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chacon and Straub, 2014</a>)</cite>.
LLM agents share a key property with software systems: both execute sequentially through discrete steps.
In software, hooks intercept function calls or events; in LLM agents, we can similarly intercept action boundaries.
Inspired by this analogy, <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> injects <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hook actions</span> at action boundaries that are triggered when the input contains a specific activation key.
These hook actions serve as auxiliary operations that do not interfere with normal actions or affect the final task output.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span> consists of two procedures: <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">injection</span> and <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">detection</span>.
Injection operates post-hoc on collected trajectories, while detection operates in a black-box setting by querying the target agent.
We present our motivation in Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Motivation ‣ 3 ActHook ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, followed by detailed injection and detection procedures.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<div id="S3.F1.2" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_bottom" style="width:176.0pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18700v1/entropy_math.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:243/217;" width="243" height="217"></object>
<p id="S3.F1.2.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.F1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a) Per-token entropy.</span></p>
</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<div id="S3.F1.3" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_bottom" style="width:162.2pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18700v1/entropy_math_relative.svg" id="S3.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:224/215;" width="224" height="215"></object>
<p id="S3.F1.3.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.F1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b) Mean entropy.</span></p>
</div></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Token entropy visualization of MATH. Computed using Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B. (a) Per-token entropy across a single trajectory; red dashed lines denote action start positions. (b) Mean entropy as a function of token position within actions. Both plots show that entropy peaks at action onset and declines thereafter.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Watermarking agent trajectory datasets faces a challenge of learnability.
Inducing an LLM to learn new patterns from a small subset of training data is difficult, as pre-trained knowledge can easily overshadow subtle signals <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rando et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Moreover, the success of watermark learning depends on the absolute number of watermarked samples rather than the ratio <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Souly et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
This poses a challenge for LLM agent trajectory datasets, which typically contain only 1–2K entries, as watermarking a substantial portion would compromise stealthiness.
Our experiments in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> confirm this: CodeMark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, a state-of-the-art code watermarking method, becomes nearly ineffective at a 5% watermark ratio.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Existing watermarks based on syntactic transformations struggle with learnability because such modifications conflict with the LLM agent trajectories’ entropy patterns <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kandpal et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
We visualize the token entropy of MATH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., </a>)</cite> trajectories in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Motivation ‣ 3 ActHook ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> to illustrate this point.
Illustrations of other datasets are deferred in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Token Entropy ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.
As shown, entropy spikes at the beginning of each action and gradually decreases as generation progresses.
This reveals that LLMs face high uncertainty only when deciding which action to take; once the action type is determined, subsequent tokens become highly predictable.
Injecting watermarks within actions, where entropy is low, forces the model to deviate from its confident predictions, making such patterns difficult to learn.
Instead of modifying tokens within actions, we insert hook actions at action boundaries where entropy is high.
Optimizing at high-entropy positions can effectively steer model behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Furthermore, hook actions can be drawn from the dataset’s existing action space, introducing no out-of-distribution content and reducing the learning objective to recognizing appropriate timing rather than memorizing rare token combinations.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S3.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text"><img src="2602.18700v1/CAW.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/171;" width="476" height="171" alt="Refer to caption"></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Overview of <span id="S3.F2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span>. <span id="S3.F2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Top)</span> The injection procedure filters valid trajectories via <math id="S3.F2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Check</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}</annotation></semantics></math>, samples a subset, and applies <math id="S3.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Inject</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}</annotation></semantics></math> to insert hook actions and append the watermark key <math id="S3.F2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> to input prompts. <math id="S3.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Inject</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}</annotation></semantics></math> involves an LLM to ensure diversity.
<span id="S3.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(Bottom)</span> The detection procedure queries a suspect model with prompts containing the key (<math id="S3.F2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>) and without, then compares hook action frequencies. A significant gap <math id="S3.F2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\Delta_{q}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>^</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\Delta_{q}}</annotation></semantics></math> indicates unauthorized dataset usage.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Overview</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">ActHook</span>, a behavior-level watermarking framework for LLM agent trajectory datasets.
Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Motivation ‣ 3 ActHook ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates the overall pipeline.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Watermark Scheme.</span>  
Central to our approach is the notion of a <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">watermark scheme</span> <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, which defines how a specific behavioral pattern can be embedded into the trained LLM agent and subsequently detected from trajectories of the trained agent.
Formally, a watermark scheme is characterized by three operations:</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}(\tau)\to\{\texttt{True},\texttt{False}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Check</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">True</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">False</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}(\tau)\to\{\texttt{True},\texttt{False}\}</annotation></semantics></math>: A predicate designed to evaluate whether a specific trajectory <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> meets the necessary structural criteria for successful watermark embedding.
For example, if our watermark is to let the agent check file existence after creation, <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Check</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}</annotation></semantics></math> verifies whether <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> contains file creation steps.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}\left(\tau\right)\to\tau^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Inject</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}\left(\tau\right)\to\tau^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>: Given a trajectory <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=\{x,(a_{1},o_{1}),\ldots,(a_{T},o_{T})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=\{x,(a_{1},o_{1}),\ldots,(a_{T},o_{T})\}</annotation></semantics></math>, this transformation produces <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> by inserting a hook action-observation pair <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a_{h},o_{h})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a_{h},o_{h})</annotation></semantics></math> at a designated position while preserving all original pairs <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(a_{n},o_{n})\}_{n=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(a_{n},o_{n})\}_{n=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> intact. Formally, <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|\tau^{\prime}|=|\tau|+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|\tau^{\prime}|=|\tau|+1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{(a_{n},o_{n})\}_{n=1}^{T}\subset\tau^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>τ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{(a_{n},o_{n})\}_{n=1}^{T}\subset\tau^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Detect}\left(\{a_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T}\right)\to\{\texttt{True},\texttt{False}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Detect</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">True</mtext><mo>,</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">False</mtext><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Detect}\left(\{a_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T}\right)\to\{\texttt{True},\texttt{False}\}</annotation></semantics></math>: A predicate that identifies whether observed actions sequences <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{a_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{a_{n}\}_{n=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> of agent trained on the watermarked trajectories matches the expected hook action pattern.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Watermark Injection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hook Action Design.</span>  
Based on whether depending on the context, hook actions can be categorized into two types: <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">standalone</em> and <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">contextual</em>.
Standalone watermarks insert hook actions that are semantically independent and can be placed at arbitrary positions within a trajectory.
For example, in code agents, we can inject a <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pwd</span> command to query the current working directory.
Standalone schemes are simpler to implement and easier for LLM to learn (as shown in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).
In contrast, contextual schemes produce natural patterns that are harder to identify through manual inspection.
In both cases, LLM-based generation achieves diverse surface forms across trajectories, encompassing varied phrasings, argument orderings, and stylistic choices. This diversity enhances stealthiness compared to rule-based approaches.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each dataset, we design hook actions drawn from its existing action distribution.
The hook action details are shown in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Watermark Details ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.
We use an auxiliary LLM to generate hook actions.
The auxiliary LLM generates standalone actions without any contextual input.
Contextual watermarks, by contrast, insert hook actions conditioned on specific trajectory elements.
In the example of file existence check after creation, the auxiliary LLM receives the file path from the preceding creation step.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Injection Procedure.</span>  
Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3.3 Watermark Injection ‣ 3 ActHook ‣ Watermarking LLM Agent Trajectories" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> details the watermark injection process.
Since <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Inject</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}</annotation></semantics></math> invokes an auxiliary LLM to generate hook actions, it incurs substantial overhead.
To minimize the number of calling auxiliary LLMs, we adopt a filter-the-sample strategy.
In Phase 1, we apply <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Check</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Check}</annotation></semantics></math> to identify all trajectories that satisfy the structural prerequisites for watermarking, yielding a candidate set <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{valid}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{valid}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This step is crucial for contextual watermarks, where only trajectories containing specific action patterns (e.g., file creation) are eligible.
In Phase 2, we compute the target watermark count <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{w}=\lfloor R\times|\mathcal{T}|\rfloor" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{w}=\lfloor R\times|\mathcal{T}|\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math> and randomly sample <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}_{select}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}_{select}</annotation></semantics></math> from the valid candidates.
In Phase 3, for selected trajectories, we invoke <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒲</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mtext class="ltx_font_smallcaps">Inject</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{W}.\textsc{Inject}</annotation></semantics></math> to insert the hook action along with its corresponding observation, and append the watermark key <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> to the user prompt as the activation trigger.
The resulting watermarked dataset, <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>, is then prepared for public release.
The watermark key <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the trigger that incentivizes hook actions.
To ensure the key does not interfere with normal agent behavior, we select phrases that are semantically neutral with respect to the task.
The key can be arbitrary and known exclusively to the dataset owner, so the hook action remains inactive during normal use and is imperceptible to users.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Watermark Injection</figcaption>

</div>

</div>

</div>
